en: The Sūtra on the Seven Daughters Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the layman Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi country during the Wu dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kuru and was staying in the Fenruda Tree Garden.
He was accompanied by a thousand arhats, five hundred bodhisattvas, as well as devas, nāgas, and spirits.
At that time, in the kingdom of Kuru, there was a brahmin named Mahā-Medha who was stingy and greedy, having no faith in the Buddha-dharma;
yet he was immensely wealthy, possessing a vast number of rare treasures, precious gems, cattle, horses, fields, and houses.
Possessing peerless wisdom, he served as the teacher for this kingdom; he constantly had five hundred disciples and was held in high esteem and honored by both the king and his ministers.
This brahmin had seven daughters who were incomparably beautiful, clever, and eloquent;
from head to foot they were adorned with gold, silver, white pearls, and necklaces, and they dressed themselves according to the season.
They were constantly accompanied by five hundred women, delighting in self-exaltation, relying on their own beauty to treat others with arrogance and pride.
Relying on his wealth and nobility, he claimed to possess constancy;
whenever he discussed the principles of righteousness with the people of the kingdom, he always emerged victorious.
At that time, there was a householder named Fenruda, who, having heard that this girl was exceedingly beautiful, went to the brahmin’s residence and said to him:
"You claim that this daughter of yours is beautiful; nevertheless, you should take her throughout the kingdom to show her to the people.
If anyone disparages this girl, you shall pay me five hundred taels of gold;
if no one disparages her, I shall pay you five hundred taels of gold."
Thus he sought for ninety days throughout the kingdom, but no one said that this girl was ugly.
At that time, the brahmin obtained five hundred taels of gold.
Bunru Da addressed the brahmin, saying:
"The Buddha is currently nearby at the Jeta Grove.
The Buddha knows the affairs of the future, the past, and the present."
"Furthermore, being sincere, I shall never speak falsely.
I must take it and show it to the Buddha. The Brahmin said:
"Excellent! he exclaimed, and immediately, together with his retinue of five hundred brahmins and another five hundred women from the kingdom, he accompanied them to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the Buddha was preaching the Dharma to many thousands of people.
Each person came forward, paid homage to the Buddha, and withdrew to sit to one side.
A brahmin then stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama, as you constantly travel through various kingdoms, have you ever seen a man so handsome and upright as this woman?
The Buddha then rebuked him:
"This woman is not beautiful; she is entirely ugly, with not a single good feature."
The brahmin asked the Buddha,
"In this entire kingdom, no one has ever said this woman was ugly.
Why, O Gautama, do you alone say that this woman is ugly?"
The brahmin asked the Buddha,
"What do people of the world consider to be good?
The Buddha said:
"If people of the world do not crave forms with their eyes and do not listen to or accept evil sounds with their ears, this is excellent;
if they do not smell fragrances with their noses and do not taste flavors with their mouths, this is excellent;
if they do not crave smooth textures with their bodies and do not harbor evil thoughts with their minds, this is excellent."
Not stealing another's wealth with one's hands and not speaking ill of others with one's mouth—this is good.
Being free from arrogance and frivolous speech, knowing where birth comes from and where death leads—this is good.
Believing that one shall obtain merit after practicing generosity—this is good.
"To have faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma, and faith in the Saṅgha of bhikṣus—this is what constitutes being 'good.
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
"Having a fine complexion does not constitute being good."
A fine body is not considered excellent;
fine clothing is not considered excellent;
and double-tongued speech and frivolous chatter are not considered excellent.
"To have a sincere heart and upright intent—this is what constitutes goodness.
Fen Rudá immediately recovered his own five hundred taels of gold.
The Buddha then addressed the Brahmin:
"In ancient times there was a city named Vārāṇasī, situated above the depths of the earth, where the Buddhas of the past and all future Buddhas sit.
At that time, there was a king named Kīrtivijaya who became a lay follower (*upāsaka*), deeply illuminated by the sūtras, and built a vihāra for the Buddha."

The king had a daughter who was a laywoman (upāsikā), learned in the scriptures and possessed of wisdom; she was peerlessly beautiful, adorned her body entirely with gold, silver, amber, and precious jewels, and was dressed in most excellent garments.

The first daughter was named Xiudān; the second daughter was named Xūdānmó; the third daughter was named Bǐqiūní; the fourth daughter was named Bǐqiūluōzhī; the fifth daughter was named Shāméní; the sixth daughter was named Shāménmì; and the seventh daughter was named Sēngdàsāndān. They constantly observed the fasts and precepts of the Buddha’s True Dharma.
Having finished giving the alms, the seven sisters took one another by the hand and went to their father the king’s main hall, where they said:
"We, sisters and brothers, wish to go together to the cemetery to wander and look about."
The king said: "The vicinity of the cemetery is most terrifying; there are only the bones and hair of the dead, with corpses strewn about and limbs scattered upon the ground;
it is filled everywhere with those who are sorrowful and those who wail."
"There are tigers, wolves, wild beasts, owls, and crows that feed primarily on the flesh and blood of the dead.
Why are you, brother and sister, staying among the graves?
Within my palace there are gardens and pavilions, bathing pools, and birds such as mandarin ducks that call out to one another."
Within it are various flowers, their five-colored radiance pleasing to the eye;
there are rare *zhi* grasses and wondrous trees, and a profusion of fruits that are pure and cool. One may eat as one pleases, and it is most excellent for wandering and viewing.
"Why are you sisters and brothers among the graves?
The seven daughters immediately replied, "Great King!
What benefit do various fruits and fine foods provide in even a ten-thousandth part [of this]?
I observe that when people in the world grow old, their lives daily hasten toward death; among those born into this world, there are none who do not die.
"We are no children, yet we have been deluded by leftover food!
If Your Majesty would compassionately take pity on us siblings, you should permit us to go outside the city to observe the dead."
Thus he spoke three times.
The King said: "Excellent!"
"I shall listen to what you sisters intend to do.
At that time, the seven daughters, together with five hundred court ladies, prepared their carriages and departed from the palace gate.

The seven daughters then untied the necklaces from their throats and scattered them upon the ground; at that moment, more than a thousand people in the kingdom saw this and followed after them to pick up the jewels.
Joyfully, he then went outside the city to the cemetery; it was foul-smelling and impure, where one could hear nothing but the sound of wailing.
The bodies of the court ladies and the common people were struck with solemn awe, and their hair stood on end.

The seven daughters went straight forward and beheld the various corpses; among them were some whose heads had been severed, some whose hands and feet had been cut off, some whose noses and ears had been sliced away; some were already dead, while others were not yet dead; some lay in cypress coffins, some were wrapped in mats, and some were bound with ropes.
The family members wept and wailed, all desiring that he be liberated from death.
The seven daughters looked around them and saw a great multitude of corpses.
Furthermore, there were those carrying dead bodies arriving from the four directions; birds and wild beasts vied with one another to come and devour them.
The dead man’s body was bloated, with pus and blood flowing out; tens of billions of worms emerged from his belly, and the stench was unbearable.
Yet the seven daughters did not even cover their noses; they walked straight forward, circumambulated him once, and then said to one another:
"Before long, the bodies of we sisters shall all become like this."
The first woman said,
"Shall we each compose a verse to save the soul of this dead man?
All six women replied:
"Excellent! The first daughter said:
"When this man was born, his body was anointed with fine perfumes and he was dressed in new, beautiful garments;..."
When walking among the crowds, she cast subtle, lingering glances;
while in the midst of people, she assumed coquettish poses, desiring that others gaze upon her.
Now she lies dead upon the ground, scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind.
"Where is the master who assumed that posture now?
The second daughter replied, "The sparrow is inside the jar; its mouth is covered, so it cannot fly out."
"Now the jar is already broken, and the sparrow has flown away.
The third daughter said, "He was traveling by carriage, but midway he abandoned the carriage and left; the carriage cannot move forward on its own."
"Where is the master who sent the carriage now?
The fourth daughter replied, "It is like a person traveling by boat; when many people are carried together across the water and reach the shore, they moor the boat."
"Abandoning the body is like abandoning a boat.
The fifth daughter said:
"There is a city, solid and strong, within which dwell many people, all of whom have been born and raised inside that city."
"Now the city is even more empty; we see no people. Where have they gone?
The sixth daughter said, "When a person dies and lies upon the ground, their clothing remains as fine as ever, from head to foot, without any deficiency."
"Now he cannot walk, nor can he move or shake.
Where, then, does that man currently reside?
The seventh daughter said:
"‘I am dwelling alone; people have left their house, and the house is empty with no one to guard it; now the house is falling into ruin.

At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra, the second king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, sat down and his seat immediately shook. Having heard the seven daughters preaching the sutra, in the time it takes to extend one’s arm, he descended from the heavens and praised the seven daughters, saying:
‘What you have said is most excellent!’"
"What do you wish to obtain?
Whatever you desire, I can procure it for you.
The seven daughters all replied:
"Are you Śakra-devānām-indra?
Or are you Brahmā-deva?
Since we did not see you approach, but you appeared naturally before us, let us know who you are."
He replied to them, "O women! I am Śakra Devānām Indra."
"I have come to hear these well-spoken and excellent words.
The seven daughters said,
"You just now wished to make a vow with us."
"You are the most honored among the gods of the second heaven, Trāyastriṃśa; you ought to obtain it for us.
We, sisters and brother, beg you to state our wishes.
The first daughter said:
"I wish to obtain a tree that has no roots, no branches, and no leaves, and to be born within it;
this is my aspiration.
The second daughter said:
"I wish to obtain a formless place upon the earth, where the boundaries of yin and yang do not exist;
I vow to be born therein. The third daughter said:
"If a person shouts loudly in the deep mountains, the sound is heard in all four directions, yet one does not know its location."
"I vow to be born therein.
Śakra Devānām-indra replied, "Stop! Do not say such things!"
"I cannot fulfill this wish of yours.
However, if you wish to become Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, or the Honored One among the sun and moon, that can indeed be attained.
As for the wish you have now made, it is truly something I do not know how to grant."
The seven daughters replied:
"You are the most honored one in heaven, possessing majestic spiritual power; why then are you unable to fulfill this vow?
You are like an old ox that cannot pull a cart nor plow the fields, providing no benefit to its master."
Śakra Devānām-indra replied:
"I have come to hear this sutra because I heard it being preached.
This is not within my knowledge; therefore, I immediately offer my apologies."
The seven daughters remained silent and gave no reply.
At that time, a deva in the air spoke, saying:
"The Buddha Kāśyapa is currently nearby, in the village of Vairambhya; why do you not go and ask him?"

Upon hearing this, the seven daughters were filled with great joy; they immediately set out together with five hundred court ladies and those who had followed to witness the scene—including five hundred others from among the mourners at the cemetery who were in a state of grief and weeping—and all resolved to go there.
"At that time, Kāśyapa Buddha was preaching the Dharma to countless thousands of people. They all came forward, paid homage to Kāśyapa Buddha, and withdrew to sit on one side.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Just now I heard the seven daughters of the king preaching the sutra, and so I have come to listen to it.'"
The seven daughters then requested this boon of me, saying:
"I wish to obtain a tree without roots, branches, or leaves;
a place without form, where there is no trace of yin or yang."
"When one shouts loudly in a deep mountain, the sound is heard in all four directions, yet one does not know its location.
At that time, I was unable to provide an answer; I pray that the Buddha will explain its meaning for the sake of the seven daughters.
Kāśyapa Buddha said: "Excellent!
Your inquiry provides great benefit and deliverance."
"Even Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas cannot know this matter, let alone you.
At that time, Kāśyapa Buddha smiled, and five-colored light issued from his mouth, illuminating the entire buddha-field, circling back around his body, and entering through the crown of his head.
The attendant knelt before him with his head bowed and asked Kāśyapa Buddha, "The Buddha does not smile without cause;
I pray that you will explain its meaning. Kāśyapa Buddha told Sāgara:
"Do you see this woman? "Yes, I have indeed seen her.

"Since these seven daughters of the king first resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they have made offerings to five hundred Buddhas and shall further serve ten thousand Buddhas. Ten kalpas hence, they shall all become Buddhas, sharing the same name, Fu-duo-luo-pei (Pūrṇabhadra), and their buddha-fields shall be named Shou-tuo-po (Śuddhābha)."
The lifespan of that Buddha was thirty thousand years; at that time, the clothing, adornments, food, and drink of the people were just like those found in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
After the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, the Dharma and the Path remained for eight thousand years before finally coming to an end.
"When that Buddha preaches the Dharma, he shall deliver seventy-five billion people, causing them to attain the path of Bodhisattvas and Arhats.

When Kāśyapa Buddha bestowed these individual predictions upon the seven daughters, they immediately leaped for joy; they then ascended into the air at a height of twenty *zhang* above the ground, and as they descended from above, they were all transformed into men and immediately attained the stage of *avaivartika*.

The five hundred court ladies and the fifteen hundred devas and humans, seeing that the seven women had been transformed into men, leaped for joy and, with great delight, all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"One thousand people were freed from dust and defilement, and all attained the Dharma-eye.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"These seven daughters of the king possess wealth and joy; they are upright and noble. Yet even they do not rely on their own bodies to create finery or beauty."
Why is this? It is because one contemplates impermanence; for this body cannot be maintained for long.
All people in the world, solely due to their ignorance, fall into the twelve links of dependent origination and thus undergo birth and death.

If human life were entirely governed by affection, then from birth one proceeds to old age; from old age, to illness; from illness, to death; and from death, to weeping, whereby one encounters suffering and pain.
If human life were entirely driven by affection and attachment, one should contemplate one’s own body and likewise contemplate the bodies of others.
Whether sitting or rising, one should reflect upon the foul secretions within the body—the tears, saliva, cold, heat, stench, and impurities.
Such is the nature of this body; when it perishes, it transforms back into worms that devour its own flesh, its bones and joints fall apart, and it is consumed into ashes and dust.
He further reflects to himself:
"When my own body dies, it shall likewise be thus.
One should not rely upon the body to create finery or beauty, but should instead contemplate impermanence.
If a person practices good deeds and does not become arrogant or engage in frivolous speech, they will all be reborn in the heavens after death;
if one practices evil deeds, they shall enter the hells.
"Why is it that women fall into the hells so frequently?
It is solely because they are possessed of jealousy and many affectations.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the Brahmin woman immediately leaped for joy; she untied the jewels from her person and scattered them over the Buddha.
Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the scattered flowers remained suspended in mid-air and were transformed into a jeweled canopy; from within it, a voice proclaimed: "Excellent!
It is no different from what the Buddha has said."
At that moment, the Buddha was moved; he manifested his majestic spiritual power and, while seated upon his throne, pressed the earth with his toe, causing the trichiliocosm to tremble violently.

His radiance illuminated the ten directions: trees that had been withered for a hundred years all bore flowers and fruit; the empty ditches and ravines were naturally filled with water; lutes and musical instruments resounded without being struck; and the pearl bracelets of the women all chimed of their own accord.

The blind regained their sight, the deaf regained their hearing, the mute regained their speech, the hunchbacked were straightened, the crippled were healed, and those with diseases of the hands and feet were cured. The insane returned to their right minds, those affected by poison found the poison no longer acting within them, and those who were imprisoned were all set free. A hundred species of birds and beasts all joined together in mournful, harmonious cries.

At that time, the people of the kingdom of Kuru—neither men nor women—were all filled with great joy, their minds harmonious toward one another as if they had attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

When the Buddha performed this miraculous transformation, the King of Kuru cast away his pearls and leaped for joy; likewise, the hundred ministers, the Brahmin girl with her retinue, and five hundred Brahmins all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, five hundred bhikṣus attained the path of Arhatship.
The five hundred people within the kingdom all attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bodhisattvas, the community of bhikṣus, the upāsakas, the upāsikās, kings, ministers, elders, the common people, devas, spirits, and nāgas were all greatly rejoiced. They came forward, placed their heads upon the ground in prostration before the Buddha, paid him homage, and departed.
The Sūtra on the Seven Daughters Spoken by the Buddha
